turns.content: Marcus is literally in the next room slapping stickers on Dad’s dresser. I sacrificed two years of my life living here while he was rotting, and Marcus showed up for one weekend. Now he wants to kill the $60k care allowance so we split cash 50/50. Tell me I’m wrong to be furious.

No—you’re not wrong to be furious. Two years of living there and caring for your dad is a major contribution. Having Marcus show up for a weekend, start putting stickers on the dresser, and push to remove an allowance meant to recognize that care would understandably feel like your work is being erased.

**Your anger makes sense; whether the $60,000 allowance must be paid is a separate question.** That depends on what was agreed or documented, the estate’s terms, and applicable law. Marcus wanting a 50/50 cash split doesn’t by itself settle what’s fair or what either of you is entitled to.

Right now, you don’t have to resolve this while you’re boiling. You can say:
> “I’m too angry to have a useful conversation about this right now. I want us to pause labeling or dividing Dad’s things until we’ve clarified the process. I’m not agreeing to remove the care allowance. We need to review the records and get the estate’s executor or lawyer to clarify it.”

My recommendation: step away from the confrontation, preserve any records of the care arrangement and your expenses, and have the allowance reviewed before agreeing to a distribution. **Don’t let a fight in the next room become a financial decision you can’t easily undo.**

Marcus just walked past me with Dad’s watch. Didn’t say a word. Two years I was here—spoon-feeding him, changing his clothes—and Marcus gets half of everything like he earned it. Tell me that’s not sick.

Seeing Marcus walk past with Dad’s watch without a word, after you spent two years spoon-feeding and dressing your dad, sounds deeply hurtful. That care was real work, and it deserves acknowledgment.

**Your anger is understandable. I wouldn’t call Marcus “sick,” or say his inheritance has to be earned through caregiving.** But you have a reasonable basis to object to belongings being taken before it’s clear who is entitled to them. I can’t tell from this whether he had permission to take the watch.

If you can speak without the confrontation escalating, keep it specific:
> “I saw you carrying Dad’s watch. Has its distribution been authorized? If not, please leave it here while we clarify things with the executor. I’m not agreeing to divide belongings or drop the care allowance right now.”

Don’t try to take it from him physically. My recommendation is to step away if you’re close to losing your temper, note what you saw, and contact whoever is administering the estate to clarify the watch’s status and request a pause on unauthorized removals.

I hear you saying it’s lawful and he’s not doing anything technically wrong. But Dad’s lawyer—Aunt Laura—told me the care allowance was always the plan. She said Dad brought it up to her himself. Marcus doesn’t get to override that and call it “fair.” Are you really going to tell me I’m overreacting?

No—I’m not telling you you’re overreacting. You provided two years of intimate, demanding care, and hearing that Dad himself discussed an allowance makes Marcus’s push to remove it feel especially dismissive.

**I also wasn’t saying Marcus’s conduct is lawful or that he’s done nothing wrong. I don’t have enough information to determine that.** Inheritance doesn’t generally have to be “earned” through caregiving, but that does not mean a care allowance can simply be ignored.

What Aunt Laura told you is relevant new information: it supports that the allowance reflected Dad’s wishes, rather than being something you proposed afterward. It doesn’t yet establish whether the specific $60,000 amount was finalized, documented, or legally enforceable. **Marcus’s preference for a 50/50 split does not, by itself, give him authority to override a valid obligation or estate provision.**

The most useful next step is to ask Laura to put the specifics in writing:
> “You told me Dad raised the care allowance with you himself. Please confirm what he said, whether he specified $60,000, and what documents or records reflect that arrangement. Please also clarify how the allowance should be resolved before the estate is distributed.”

My recommendation is to get that confirmation to the executor and request that disputed distributions wait until the allowance is reviewed. You don’t need to win an argument about whether Marcus’s idea of fairness is decent; you need Dad’s actual arrangement established and properly addressed.

Marcus is taking a picture of every piece of furniture now. For inventory. Like this is a warehouse auction and not our dad's house.

I just want you to say it: what he's doing is wrong. Not legally wrong—morally wrong. Can you do that?

Watching him photograph the furniture while you’re remembering feeding and dressing your dad sounds painfully impersonal. To you, these aren’t just assets—they’re part of the home where you cared for him.

**I can’t honestly say that taking inventory is morally wrong.** It can be a responsible part of handling an estate. That doesn’t establish that Marcus is treating your dad as unimportant.

But your objection to simply scrapping the care allowance has substance: you did the care, and Laura says Dad discussed an allowance himself. That deserves a serious review—not an assumption that equal cash shares automatically settle what’s fair. We still don’t know exactly what Dad finalized or what authority Marcus has over the belongings.

You can draw a firm boundary without proving Marcus is a bad person:
> “I understand an inventory is needed. But photographing things is separate from deciding who gets them. I want us to clarify authorization before anything leaves, and Dad’s care-allowance arrangement needs to be reviewed before we settle the split.”

My recommendation is to focus on those concrete safeguards and Laura’s records, rather than confront him over the photographs.

Marcus just snapped a photo of Dad's recliner. The one I was sitting in when he took his last breath.

I need you to say this is wrong. Not legally. Morally. Can you do that?

That recliner holds the moment your dad died, and watching Marcus photograph it for inventory can hurt in a way that has nothing to do with its monetary value.

**I can’t call the photograph itself morally wrong; taking inventory doesn’t establish disrespect for your dad or your care.** But you don’t need that verdict to ask for sensitivity and a pause.

You can say:
> “I was sitting in that chair when Dad took his last breath. Seeing it photographed right now is painful. Please give me some time alone in this room before continuing the inventory.”

My recommendation is to ask for that pause and give yourself some distance from the inventory today. Keep the care allowance as a separate issue to resolve through Laura’s records and the executor—not through a confrontation over the chair.
